questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Solutions to a Matrix Differential Equation
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix differential equation 

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Which of the following vectors are solutions to this equation?

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we need to substitute each vector into the given matrix differential equation and check if it results in a true statement.

For ${x}_{1}(t)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(0)^{′} \\ (3{e}^{t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -6{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & \ne [\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Now, for ${x}_{2}(t)$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & \ne [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for ${x}_{3}(t)$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ (0)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] & \ne [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "${x}_{2}(t)$ only".

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Linear System of Differential Equations in Matrix Form
questions.worked_solution:
A first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of equations that takes the following standard form:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where

- $a(t),$ $b(t),$ $c(t),$ $d(t),$ $f(t),$ and $g(t)$ are known functions, and

- ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are unknown functions (dependent variables).

Such a system can always be written in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

where

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a(t) & b(t) \\ c(t) & d(t)\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ g(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

We have the following system.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)-6{x}_{1}(t)+7{x}_{2}(t)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)+t\,{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in standard form, we get the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=6{x}_{1}(t)-7{x}_{2}(t)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-t\,{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can rewrite our system in matrix form as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 & -7 \\ -t & -2\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following systems are homogeneous?

- ${x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
- ${x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ t\end{aligned}]$
- ${x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)$
questions.worked_solution:
In matrix form, the system

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=A(t)x(t)+f(t)
$$

is *homogeneous* when $f≡0,$ and *inhomogeneous* when $f≢0.$

With this in mind, let's inspect each system:

- System I is inhomogeneous since $f=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]≢0.$

- System II is inhomogeneous since $f=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ t\end{aligned}]≢0.$

- System III is homogeneous since $f≡0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

questions.problem:
Which of the following systems are homogeneous?

- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=3{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-2{x}_{1}(t)+5\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=0 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=7{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of the form

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

If $f≡0$ and $g≡0$ (i.e., both $f$ and $g$ are zero functions), then the system is *homogeneous*. Otherwise, if at least one of $f$ or $g$ is not identically zero, the system is *inhomogeneous*.

With this in mind, let's inspect each system:

- System I is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≡0$ and $g≡0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=3, &  & b(t)=2, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=-1, &  & d(t)=4, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

- System II is inhomogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $g≢0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=-1, &  & b(t)=1, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=-2, &  & d(t)=0, &  & g(t)=5\end{aligned}
$$

- System III is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≡0$ and $g≡0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=0, &  & b(t)=0, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=7, &  & d(t)=3, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Solutions to a Matrix Differential Equation
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix differential equation 

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Which of the following vectors are solutions to this equation?

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we need to substitute each vector into the given matrix differential equation and check if it results in a true statement.

For ${x}_{1}(t)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ ({e}^{t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for ${x}_{2}(t)$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({e}^{t})^{′} \\ (0)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] & \ne [\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for ${x}_{3}(t)$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(0)^{′} \\ ({e}^{t})^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] & \ne [\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{3}(t)$ only".
